items.title: Finding the Brain’s Mood Switch in Bipolar Disorder
items.snippet: What causes the sudden transition between depression and mania in bipolar disorder? Researchers at USC, Stanford, and Johns Hopkins received a $4.5M BD² grant to study "retrosplenial switch cells"—a unique neuronal population that may control mood switching.

items.title: How Ego and Self-Image Change Brain Sync
items.snippet: Why do some individuals struggle with genuine empathy? Brain scans show that people with high grandiose traits fail to synchronize their brain activity with others when watching someone lose face or experience social vulnerability.

items.title: Walking Speed Sharpens Visual Sensitivity to Backward Motion
items.snippet: Why is the brain extra sensitive to backward motion while walking? Research shows that at typical walking speeds, our visual system detects smaller speed changes in contracting optic flow, functioning as a vital reflex to prevent backward falls.

items.title: Why the Left Brain Controls the Right Body
items.snippet: Why does the left side of your brain control the right side of your body? Neuroscientists at the University of Minnesota propose that the brain’s cross-wiring originated from the optical inversion of ancient eyes, which forced motor and sensory circuits to follow a contralateral map over 500 million years ago.

items.title: Wearable Vagus Nerve Devices Rewire Depressive Brains
items.snippet: Vagus nerve stimulation is a proven treatment for depression, but it has historically required surgery. A comprehensive review in Med-X shows how wearable ear and neck bioelectronics are transforming non-invasive VNS into an accessible, AI-guided home therapy.

items.title: Could tomato paste help your brain? A three-month trial points to modest gains in attention and memory
The hard part of belonging begins after you’ve found your people
items.snippet: Drawing on psychiatrist Murray Bowen’s family systems theory, Henri Tajfel’s minimal group experiments, and Gustave Le Bon’s study of crowds, Luke Burgis separates the “solid self” from the “pseudo self” that reshapes itself for every room, and how to preserve your truest essence. This video The hard part of belonging begins after you’ve found your people is featured on Big Think .
